utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everyone. Madam Registrar, could you kindly call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. For the record all the accused are present. All the Defence teams, every member, is present. Prosecution is Mr. McCloskey and Mr. Thayer. Now, we've got three problems. One is that we've already lost 20 minutes because of the technical problems that we had, and these 20 minutes happen to be very precious, given the circumstances. The second is, I don't know if you have had further discussions amongst yourself to resolve the issue that I foresaw coming yesterday, namely what's going to happen with the next witness, the Defence expert witness. Yes, Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, good afternoon, Your Honours, good afternoon, everyone. Mr. President, we have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before you continue, Mr. Thayer, sorry to interrupt you like this, but we are, as you may have noticed Judge Prost will be with us -- Judge Stole will be with us after the first session. He's got something personal that cropped up that he has to attend to and he'll certainly make it by the end of this session. So we are sitting pursuant to Rule 15 bis. Yes, Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think I can get right down to the gist of the matter. I think we are going to need some Solomonic guidance from the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's what we were discussing and hopefully not needing to resort to.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Well, we have been engaged in numerous communications to try to resolve it and we actually thought we had a very workable and unanimously satisfactory solution that we were about an inch away from completing yesterday, which was, given certain problems that I had been alerted to by some of my friends with respect to securing the extended visa and expert fees and so forth that had been unexpected for Mr. Rodic, given the likelihood of those difficulties, we had come up with a plan to stop or temporarily interrupt Mr. Trivic's testimony at the end of the day today so that we could continue -- or we could begin and complete Mr. Rodic's testimony in the two days which I think everybody agrees we can do. That was ultimately contingent upon Mr. Trivic agreeing to that unanimously agreed plan. He is firm that he wishes to go home and complete his testimony while he's here. We won't hold that against him. That's his decision. That is the rock. The hard place that we are caught between now is Mr. Rodic has advised my friends that he fears that he will lose his job if he is required to appear on Tuesday should his testimony not be completed. Now, and I've engaged in some discussion with my friends about this topic specifically as well. I think our experience has been that when we receive that type of information, frequently and in this trial it's been the case that when the Chamber makes it clear or suggests that it has an expectation that a witness is available for a particular day, when that gets communicated to the employer, whether it's been the Dutch Ministry of Defence or another employer, that that has a salutary effect. However, in this case I'm being told that Mr. Rodic has a private employer that may be more inured to the Court's statements on this topic. So that is where we are. We really don't have any further suggestions than that. We could continue with Mr. Trivic's testimony, complete his testimony, begin Mr. Rodic's testimony, and see how far we get by the end of the day on Thursday and if we are not done cross-examining him, we can bring him back at the earliest. Our collective preference was to begin and end Mr. Rodic's testimony as soon as possible. We understand that that is among the highest of priorities for everyone to get this intercept issue resolved. So I think that's where we are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's take it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's take it bit by bit. Mr. Krgovic, how much more time you need for your cross-examination of Mr. Trivic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I will do my best, Your Honour. I think I will reduce my cross and I think I will have half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Haynes?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I think I've asked for an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, you have.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: But you should know that the schedule of documents that I will serve in a short while contains no fewer than 24 documents for this witness. I have nine separate headings of cross-examination for him, and I think an hour is very optimistic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Madam Fauveau? You requested two hours.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. I would do my best to finish in less time, maybe an hour 30, an hour 45 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic? Thank you, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: As for Mr. Borovcanin's Defence it is very likely that we will have no cross-examination for this witness. However, I cannot guarantee right this moment and we made an agreement among ourselves that Madam Fauveau will go first and if she covers all the topics that we have, then we'll have no cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President. The situation is the same with respect as the Borovcanin team, that is, although we had requested half an hour, we anticipate that all the questions that we wanted to ask will have been asked by the end. But of course I cannot say at this time and foreclose or say that I will not have a short cross-examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Meek?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. We have the -- we take the same position as Mr. Bourgon and believe we'll have no cross-examination but don't want to close the door on it, either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I believe that 20 minutes will be enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we are talking of three hours and 20 minutes, the least. That's the most optimistic scenario. So let's -- I suggest we go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think the best way to go is to proceed with the testimony of Mr. Trivic and hopefully we try to manage the sitting in a way as to call upon you to make an extra effort, those who will be cross-examining, to finish by today. Then there is this other aspect that regards Mr. Rodic, and this is an expert witness for five of the accused, five Defence teams. And still we see that there are five requests for an examination-in-chief. Our suggestion to you - and this is by way of trying to come forward with something practical that could perhaps make it possible for Mr. Rodic to finish his testimony by the end of Thursday - is to liaise amongst yourselves, the five of you, and there will only be one of you that will examine the expert in chief, with the understanding that if there are any leftovers that come to your mind en passant, as we go along, then, of course, you will have the opportunity to put the questions but ideally, you should agree amongst yourself what questions to put and there will just be one of you that will examine this witness in chief, and you will then be able to establish, to estimate the time you require. That's one. Obviously, the Gvero team had indicated that they wish to cross-examine this expert and you will have every opportunity to do so. The Pandurevic team have indicated no intention to cross-examine the witness and of course you will have cross-examination. So if you think this is workable, then perhaps we can adopt this system. You can have one day, complete day for your examination-in-chief and the Prosecution will have another day minus ten minutes which will be reserved for the Gvero Defence team. Think about it. We don't want to know now. Let's proceed so as not to lose more time. And perhaps the first break you will tell us. While the witness is arriving, following the -- I know that Mr. Bourgon wishes to address the Trial Chamber to clarify something about the Defence motion he filed yesterday, but before he does so, there are two urgent issues that arise out of that motion, namely the request of the Defence for interim provisions to be taken. Since they -- in particular as regards Witnesses PW-108 and 128, we are not in a position--

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Usher? We are not in a position to wait much and we wish to hand down our decision by the end of this week. We are calling upon you, Mr. McCloskey, Mr. Thayer, to file a response limited to that part of the motion namely the last part, the interim -- the request for the interim provisions by no later than the end of tomorrow, office hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Nicholls is working on that and we should be able to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. The other thing is this: Reading through your motion, Mr. Bourgon, now it seems very obvious to us that in order to be able to evaluate some of the submissions that you're making, particularly that what is contained in the witness summary provided by the Prosecution does not tally with what the witness had previously stated in his witness statement, we now definitely require the witness statement to go through it to be able to make an assessment of your submission. So since we had decided earlier to expunge that witness statement from the record, and yesterday we had a confirmation that the witness statement has indeed been expunged through a special procedure, we now want it back. There is no way in -- we can ask Mr. Pimentel to do the whole exercise and go in reverse mode. So Mr. McCloskey, please, could you also let us have a copy of that witness statement again tomorrow, together with or separately but no later than the end of the day tomorrow? That's about it. Now, Mr. Bourgon, you intimated that you need to address us to clarify something about your motion. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Indeed, Mr. President, very quickly. There are corrections I'd like to bring on the record concerning the motion. At paragraph 119, subparagraph C and as well as footnote 36. This paragraph relates to the 11 witnesses -- Mr. President, I need to go into closed session for this, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go into private session for a short while.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Trivic, good afternoon to you, sorry for having -- for keeping you waiting. Yes, Mr. Meek?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. President, before we start I just want you to know before 4.00 the Beara Defence team will be filing a joinder, a short joinder to that motion, that's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. The more the merrier, sort of. Yes, Mr. Trivic, good afternoon to you and my apologies to you for having kept you waiting but we had some procedural matters to attend to. We'll now proceed, Mr. Krgovic. We will do our best to finish with your testimony today. Mr. Krgovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: We broke off yesterday when I asked you whether you remembered the entry into Srebrenica on the 11th and the state of affairs as you found it in Srebrenica. I asked you about the hospital, but did you pass by the post office? Did you have occasion to look at the post office building in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There isn't anything in particular that sticks in my mind. I saw the hospital. I'm not sure about the post office.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have occasion to enter the UN base in Srebrenica near to the petrol station there?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Did you notice any shelling marks within the base compound or in the yard itself?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't notice any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Let us briefly go back to your yesterday's answers. And it has to do with your brief conversation with General Gvero. The reason why you approached General Gvero was the morale levels in your unit and this is something that is within the purview of the officer for morale?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, yes. That is one of the duties discharged by such officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: When you answered my question which had to do with the plans entertained by some UNPROFOR members to provoke Serbs, do you know that generally speaking, in Republika Srpska at the time, it was known that UNPROFOR forces were trying to find a way of provoking Serbs in order to have a reason to launch air strikes and were you aware of this and were you aware of the fact that also for this reason you were to refrain from any attacks against UNPROFOR members?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, based on the intelligence that arrived from superior commands and based on the intelligence we received from the people out afield, there was some mention of it. Later on, as I studied some documents, I came to know, based on General Smith's statement, that he, in fact, proposed it to the UN units themselves, or rather, the UN representative who was to convey this to the Security Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: When you were preparing for your testimony in the Blagojevic case, it was at that time that you learnt this?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was also studying the military, political and other matters, and in particular, when I was working and preparing for the Krajisnik case. I was also in touch with some Defence counsel when I stated that I was prepared to appear as a Defence witness in this particular case too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: On the 11th, you received an assignment to secure certain lines and features. Let me show you a document now from the Drina Corps command which, among its addressees also has your unit. Can we have P439 shown to the witness, please? This is an order dated 11th of July. Could you please read the paragraph above the line where it says, "Order." It is quite obvious that the order was also sent to your unit.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And to the 2nd Romanija Brigade as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: "With a view to preventing the return of the Muslim forces into Srebrenica, I issue the following order." Do you see that section of the document?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Can we just scroll down a bit? In this particular order, it is stated that the morale -- the combat readiness had to be raised to the highest level, that ambushes had to be set, cooperation with MUP had to be ensured, and units and positions had to be secured. Is this consistent with the assessments you received from the ground?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: After the cessation of combat activities around Srebrenica, what was your knowledge as to the effect how and why the civilian population was being evacuated? Can you tell us something about what you knew of how the evacuation of the civilian population came about?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In answer to a question by the Prosecution, I said that my only knowledge of evacuation on that particular date was on the basis of my own assessment and expectations, and when in the command of the Bratunac Brigade General Mladic spoke to someone over the phone, and I overheard this conversation, which had to do with the procurement of means of transportation and fuel, I learnt more about it later on, but at the time I didn't know anything else, save, of course, for what I was able to observe of the evacuation on my way to Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Did you know that an agreement had been reached with the representatives of the civilian authorities in Srebrenica and that an agreement had been signed and that General Mladic offered the Muslim population to choose whether they wanted to stay or leave and that they decided to evacuate themselves from Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was something we were briefly informed on during a briefing in Bratunac, but I did not have any specific assignments in that regard and I didn't give it particular thought, but I know that commanders were briefed to that extent and to that effect, to know what was going on in the area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please allow a short pause before you start answering Mr. Krgovic's questions so that the interpreters can catch up with their translation. Yes, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour. It's my fault I'm trying to be as speedy as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm glad you got the message, even though I addressed the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: On the 13th, you set out into the Zepa area. Did you receive information, upon your arrival there, about the enemy forces you were going to be facing? Were you given an estimate as to their strength and weapons they had, as was indeed the case at the earlier briefing prior to the action in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The -- there was an estimate that there were around 1500 to 2.000 armed members of ABiH there, in the area of Zepa, that these forces had organised their defences and that some 500 to 700 people were estimated to have arrived from the Srebrenica enclave after our forces had entered Srebrenica. These were elements of their forces who refused to disarm and set out from Srebrenica toward Zepa, so I suppose that there were around two to 2.500 members of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Did you receive any instructions as to how you were to treat UNPROFOR members and the civilian population?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The general position that had been conveyed from the superior command, and which we as brigade commanders conveyed down the chain of command, was that in any combat activity, UNPROFOR forces should not be attacked, that the aim of those activities was to engage armed forces. This position had always been presented to us in all the assignments, including this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown Exhibit P114? This is an order to launch an attack against the Zepa enclave dated the 13th of July. Could we please turn to page 3 in the B/C/S and page 4 in the English version? Can we scroll down, please? Very well. Sir, look at the paragraph starting, "Civilian Muslim population and UNPROFOR are not the objective of the operation of our forces." Have you found that passage?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Is this consistent with the instructions you received on the spot?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, the orders I received followed from this one, as this is a document that would normally be kept with the headquarters of the unit issuing the order.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: In your combat activities, as far as you know, and as far as your units are concerned, you adhered to these orders?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did. Throughout combat activities, I didn't have any contacts with UNPROFOR forces in the Zepa area, although I must say that the UN APC which was at a hill in the settlement of Borak was used by the BiH army to fire upon our forces. I conclude this because fire had been opened from the APC upon us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown 6D82, please? The document before you is a report on intelligence concerning the enemy in the enclaves of Zepa and Gorazde dated the 20 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Yes, the 24th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Could we scroll down, please? Very well. I'm interested in the bottom part, the sentence starting with, "At any rate or at any event. It has been four days now that the Muslims have been firing from heavy anti-aircraft machine-guns." There is a brief description of the weaponry used and activities launched in that period. Is this description of the weapons used by them at the time consistent with what you know, from what you knew on the ground?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of the fire our forces had to put up with at that time from the fortification on the elevation at Borak, I can say that this is consistent with this particular piece of intelligence obtained by our intelligence officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Can we please go back to the top part of the document? A bit down, further down, please. There is one passage here which starts, and it's in the middle of the second paragraph, "The Muslim forces have engaged and included into their firing system the UNPROFOR hardware and weaponry which they laid their hands on during the recent blockade."

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see this part.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: It's in the middle part, "The Muslim forces have also included the UNPROFOR hardware and weapons."

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Is this consistent with the fire opened from the APC on your forces?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was this one APC on the elevation at Borak which opened fire on my forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: The document goes on to say, and can we look at page 2, please? In the second paragraph, toward the bottom, which says that the civilian population, particularly in the central area of the enclave, that's fifth line from the top.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Is there consistent with your knowledge that they had evacuated the civilian population out of the combat area of your forces?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is consistent because later on, it became clear when we came out at Zepska Koliba, the houses there, there were still traces of the civilian population having been there previously at that plateau.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: As you advanced in the Zepa area, how did you mark your own units as they were on the move?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We mostly set hay alight and in one case there was a wooden cottage or a hut. As we were trying to seize the stronghold organised at Vis and the Borak hamlet, that was this particular case where we set this hut alight; otherwise we would set fire to hay so that the operations commander who was observing the operation from the observation post would be able to follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: This served for you to identify the positions of units?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because the configuration of the terrain was such as did not allow a line of visibility further than four to 500 metres, and the observation post was closer to, let's say, Rogatica and a bit further from Han Pijesak for the operation was taking place the following day. This was a way of making sure that they could follow the advance of the units. We had to use these, "Indian signs," in order to know where the units advanced.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: At one point, did not the Muslim forces also set fire to a feature?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't talk about whether the Muslim forces set something on fire. I know that General Krstic intervened and asked us to act responsibly because several houses had been set on fire. This was in the evening hours. And I was warned that I would be held responsible personally unless I identified the perpetrators, those who set those houses on fire and punished them. Ultimately, it became clear that none of my units were responsible for this. I don't know whether this was done by the defenders, by the ABiH forces of Zepa.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, your 30 minutes will come to an end in about eight minutes' time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, did you make note of this in your diary?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The entire incident involving the warning that I was given by the operations commander, my subsequent inquiry which enabled me to report back to General Krstic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Let me take you back to one stage at the end of -- toward the end of the operation. At one point you were wounded in Zepa. This was after the signing of the agreement and after the evacuation of the civilian population, when the fighting continued; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. My unit was given the mission to break through to Zepska Koliba and I was wounded on the 29th, near the communications centre at Zlovrh, below that centre, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Let -- I will show you a document, 6D125. This is a document, information about the attack on Srebrenica. Can we look at the bottom part? Let us read a couple of paragraphs and you will tell me if the contents of this document reflects what happened on the ground. This document is ascribed to General Gvero. It's dated 10 July. It's a typo here. It's not June. It's July, 1995. In paragraph 2, we read that the area of Srebrenica was to be demilitarised in keeping with the agreement that had been signed, and that all military and paramilitary units were to be withdrawn with all weapons surrendered. That was not done?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: So this passage is correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It certainly is. In view of the fact that the forces of the 28th Division continued to occupy positions in the area of Srebrenica and its members lived there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: So the UNPROFOR did not carry any of this out, it didn't disarm Muslim forces and the Muslim forces continued to supply themselves with arms, they continued -- they committed major crimes, acting out of the zone --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Haven't we heard about this already from I don't know how many witnesses? And I dare even think that this was something that the Prosecution themselves acknowledged. It's one of the agreed facts. I mean, do we have to go through all this again?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. If the Prosecutor agrees. We actually tried to agree with the Prosecution about this document and it -- the attempt was not successful. That's why I wanted to go through it briefly. I have just one more question in connection with this document. Could we show page 2? Sorry, page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Look at this passage in paragraph 2. "Our current combat activities are only geared at neutralising Muslim terrorists. They are not targeting civilians." Is this consistent with what you know and what you yourself did in the Srebrenica operation and Zepa operation?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Like any army, I suppose in the world, in all the wars, the army to which I belonged never had as its objective to target civilian population, and in this particular case it didn't target UNPROFOR members either.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: If you had occasion to briefly look through this document, did you find anything in it that is a lie, that is inaccurate?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what I was able to see so far, there is nothing that would be a lie.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: My last question: Can we see 6D127, please? This is a combat report of 15th July. Could we scroll down, please? This is a combat report of the 15th of July from which we see that you signed it. It's in fact a telegram. Were you at the command on the 15th of July? Did you send and sign this combat report?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, at the command. Maybe it was sent from the forward command post, but I was not at the command at Knezina, at the original location.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: The fact that your name is signed here, does it mean that you signed this document?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it doesn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Is it possible that when somebody signs and adds "for" Mirko Trivic, is it possible that the recipient would not see the signature, that they would only see the typed part?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wouldn't be visible because this was obviously encrypted and sent by fax -- not by fax. It was encrypted and sent that way, so it wouldn't be visible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And on the 15th, you were obviously in Zepa?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in the Zepa area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: So you couldn't have signed this document?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I see in my notes that I have one more short question for this witness left, just three minutes perhaps, and that will be the end of my cross-examination. Mr. Trivic, do you know General Miletic?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that Mr. Miletic's wife is Croat and she has Croat citizenship?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And his daughter is also of Croat citizenship?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under the laws in former Yugoslavia, all children born in a certain republic receive the citizenship of that republic regardless of the current location of their parents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Trivic. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you for that, Mr. Krgovic, and for your cooperation. Mr. Haynes? Are you going next?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: No. I think in light of the fact that Madam Fauveau estimates that she has two hours, we thought it was better that she complete her cross-examination today and rule out the risk of somebody being divided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Madam Fauveau, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, last Friday, you said that in end June, beginning of July, you started other preparations for actions in Srebrenica. I'm speaking about the end of June, July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In end June or beginning of July.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Could we show the witness P106?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: While that is being done, Madam Fauveau, we'll have the break at 16 hours and five minutes and it will be a shortened break this time, with your indulgence. Instead of 25 minutes, 20 minutes, try to recover a little bit of the time lost. And then you will continue at 1645.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, the copy is not very good but could you confirm, please, that this order before you is indeed the preparatory order that you received and it's dated 2nd July? Could we just show the top of the document, please?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is the preparatory order. And that is recorded in one of the brigade commands but it was encrypted.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, for the moment what I'm interested in is this: Can we say that this preparatory order was issued by the Drina Corps command?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And if we look at the first paragraph of this order, is it correct that this first paragraph relates to a major offensive of the enemy that began in mid-March?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. One can see that in item 1, and this reflects the situation that existed at the time when the agreement was signed in the spring -- or rather in the winter time of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And this offensive of the enemy mentioned in this paragraph was a Muslim offensive launched on a number of fronts against Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That can be seen from the introductory part of the preparatory order.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And according to what is written in the following paragraph, we see that this offensive took place in the areas of the 2nd Krajina Corps, the area of the Sarajevo corps, the area of the Drina Corps and the east Bosnia corps area.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're reading paragraph 2, the 1st Sarajevo, Romanija, Herzegovina and eastern Bosnian corps are mentioned, and it was expected that the enemy was going to be active in Kladanj and Olovo, in the area of responsibility of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it true that the areas covered by the 3rd Corps cover almost the entirety of Republika Srpska territory?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you remember of this Muslim offensive that was launched in mid-March 1995?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were offensives in different areas, among others in the spring of 1995 an offensive was launched from the Tuzla area, I believe, toward the eastern Bosnian corps and Drina Corps areas. I had to send elements of my units to help in the area of the Zvornik Brigade, if I remember correctly, because that particular brigade was under attack in its own zone.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You can see at the top of this document the units, in fact brigades, to which this order was addressed. Is it correct that this order, in fact, all the units, addressees, were the units of the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In paragraph 3, the Zvornik Brigade, the 1st Bratunac Brigade, the 1st and the 5th Podrinje light infantry brigades, yes, in fact these units were parts of the Drina Corps. The units to which this order was addressed were all part of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And to the best of your knowledge, in fact, from what you see written in this preparatory order, this order was not brought to the notice of the Main Staff of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because such orders do not make it incumbent upon the commander to send it to the superior command. This is something that is within his discretion. He sends this order in order to inform subordinate units of what they can expect in the forthcoming period.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Can we show the witness page 2 of this order? Sir, do you see item 5, para 5? Is it true that in conformity with para 5, all the preparations for this operation had to be performed by the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The corps command was to carry out all the preparations for activities from the forward command post and would make it operational by the 4th of July.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it true that as a result of this preparatory order, you also received executive orders to move your troops into battle?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Can we show the witness Exhibit P107? Is it the order on the basis of which the operation around Srebrenica took place?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: This order was sent to the units involved in the operation?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was handed out when assignments were being issued upon the arrival in the area where combat activities were to take place.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And the units that are enumerated here, at the beginning of this document, are, in fact, the units that participated in the operation around Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And this order was not notified from what we see in the document to the Main Staff of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no need for that. The order by commander is not sent up, since the decision approving these activities had been issued, I'm not saying that the Main Staff did not need to know about this but the activities were approved and the document is issued for the purposes of the subordinate units and stays with the issuing headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Can we see the lower part of the page? That's perfect. Is it correct that item 1 of this order describes the situation in the zone of the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was an assessment by the corps command. I cannot make it different in any way. If this was something that was produced by commanders who were aware of the situation on the ground, then the receiving subordinate units would only take notice of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And according to what is written in para 1 of this order, the enemy was mounting attacks against the units of the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, from the protected zone, as was said in the preparatory order, particularly intensified were the activities in the last or toward the end of those four months when a cease-fire had been agreed, the corps command and the forces were provoked to react by the many victims among the civilian population and also among members of the units which set out to separate the areas.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Similarly, the Drina Corps had information that the forces of the 28th Division intended to cut the area of the Drina Corps in two and link up with the eastern forces?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that on the basis of intelligence received, and assessments of the command, such a conclusion was reached and they were guided by these conclusions as they were preparing for action.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Can we show the witness page 2 of this order? In English, it's page 3. Can we see the lower part of the page, para 4? You have spoken on Friday about the objective of this operation around Srebrenica. Can you see the second paragraph in item 4? It states the objective of this operation around Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And according to this order, the objective of the operation was to separate the enclaves Srebrenica from Zepa and to reduce the size of the enclaves as well as to create conditions necessary to eliminate them.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That transpires clearly from the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Can we now show the top part, para 2, of the order? Yes. This is the middle, in fact. In para 2 of this order, the Drina Corps command, in fact the commander who issued this order, invokes directive 7 and 7/1.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it correct that you were aware of this directive 7 and directive 7/1?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The brigade commands did not receive the contents of the directives, but undoubtedly the corps commands did, through the general guidelines, based on the directives, the corps command, which produces an autonomous assessment of the situation within its area of defence or let me use the synonym, area of responsibility, the corps command makes the decision by invoking the instructions contained in the directive.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I would like to show the witness P5, but maybe we can put it on the ELMO so the witness can have it before him. P5. Maybe in e-court we can leave document, P107, and we can put P5 on the ELMO. I'm sorry about this. And could we put page 2 on the e-court document so we can see para 2? Sir, what you have next to you on the ELMO, is that directive number 7?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can see, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Could we say that this directive was issued by the Supreme Command of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I saw the heading, which says that the Supreme Command issued the directive number 7.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you know that this directive states the tasks of the -- states the objectives of the VRS as determined by the Supreme Command?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But let me explain my position, if I may be allowed. A directive is not a simple document. It's not a mission or a task. A directive is issued as an instruction on how to proceed. It's guidance given for the forthcoming period. It results from an analysis of the Supreme Command of the situation on the entire battlefield in Republika Srpska. Accordingly, it is formulated in accordance -- or rather, it is formulated as general instructions to the army and depending on the situations in different front lines also to the corps commands, in particular front lines. It's a document issued by the Supreme Command, by army commands, according to the procedure we adhered to and complied with during the war in Republika Srpska, throughout the war. I apologise. If I can only say this: This is exactly how things were done. One would make an assessment of the other side and then -- and that would be the basis for the directive that was sent to the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Can we now show the witness page 8 of the directive? It is the page marked is 8. And it's -- the last digits of the ERN number are 3173. And in English it's page 10. Could we see the lower part of this page? Just a little bit further down. Perfect. Thank you. Can you see the paragraph that begins with the word, "The Drina Corps"? Is it correct that this part of the directive sets out in greater precision the instructions given to the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This part relates to the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I would now like to ask you to read the first paragraph, the one that starts after the heading, "Drina Corps" and to compare it with para 2 of the 2nd July order that you see on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The Drina Corps, with a highly persistent and active defence, with elements of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps units, in the northwestern part of the battlefield and around the enclave is to prevent the break-throughs of the enemy in -- along certain selected operational, tactical axes, with demonstrative and active combat activities by applying measures of operational and tactical camouflage, carry out as strong as possible actions toward the enclaves." Should I read further?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Can we now see the bottom of page 2 so that the witness can see para 2 in its entirety?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it correct that this order envisaged reducing the enclaves to the urban area?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Separation and narrowing down.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And that separation is planned in that directive, but the reduction or the narrowing down isn't envisaged by the directive?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Could we then say that the 2nd July order went beyond what was written in the directive?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Let me explain. The Drina Corps command invokes only the directive as an instruction to take certain measures to prevent activities and break-throughs out of the enclave. And you see this part of the order that the command of the Drina Corps, pursuant to the directive, makes an independent decision because they did not use the part involving coordinated action with Sarajevo Romanija Corps, because the directive stated that this should be done in coordinated with action. They decided not to proceed this way, because they did not want to wait for the Main Staff to take measures to involve both the Sarajevo Romanija Corps and the Drina Corps to deal with the enclave. Rather, it was on their own discretion that they used the free forces, as they put it, and these are parts of the 2nd Romanija Corps which were not tied up with other forces, they were available units and they used these available units without coordinated action with other corps, including the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, and autonomously set out to accomplish the mission with the approval of the commander of the Main Staff. Therefore, they autonomously decided on how to proceed. They merely used the document as the basis for making such a decision, namely the directive.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it correct that, in fact, if the 2nd July order represented an execution of the directive, the 2nd Corps command should have written precisely the same thing that was written in the instructions handed out to the Drina Corps in the directive?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You said the 2nd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: The commander of the Drina Corps should have written in para 2 of his order exactly the same thing that was written in the directive?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm going back again to the significance and the role of the directive in the formulation of these assignments. The directive only serves as guidance for a period of one year and the commanders take out parts of it that they, according to their assessment, can carry through. There were situations when none of the guidelines given in a directive were, in fact, carried out. It wasn't a binding document. Had it been binding, then the Sarajevo Romanija Corps should have had to be involved in coordinated action.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Could you now please look at the sentence where you just stopped reading a moment ago concerning that directive? It's the sentence that begins with, "... by planned and well-thought-out."

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the sentence that follows the passage I read. "By daily planned and well-thought-out combat activities create conditions of total uncertainty and absence of any prospect for further existence as well as intolerable conditions for the life of locals in Srebrenica and Zepa."

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you agree that this has a particular significance in military terminology?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the situation in that area was also very particular and peculiar. I suppose that the Supreme Command made its own analysis in certain theatres of war, and there were particular problems with organising security against attacks from protected areas. Therefore, I believe that this has something to do with normal treatment of forces that keep a part of the population encircled in one of the theatres of war in Republika Srpska. Namely, the doctrine with which we went to war envisaged combat on one's own territory. Those activities, that combat, also included encircling enemy forces, in this case the forces of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina had several locations where they were organised at the time when the political leadership won the political recognition for Bosnia's independence and left those forces of the then-proclaimed independent Bosnia and Herzegovina in areas where the population did not have any choice whether they wanted to stay or go. In this case, the population was trapped in those areas that were proclaimed protected areas with the arrival of the UN force. The army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the UN force as well were responsible for the future fate of that population. To carry out the demilitarisation, to create a situation where the population can be given the choice whether to go or to stay in Republika Srpska, this kind of sanction was applied that is still applied in the world today, when one's own civilian population is trapped so that somebody can realise their political goals. So in this area, a population was encircled by the enemy and within the doctrine that we, not only we, applied, this is nothing special. Since normal life was not possible anyway, this population had to be put in a position where they would have to choose where they wanted to live, because this was obviously an area of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it correct that this sentence within a military logic cannot be interpreted as a plan of attack on civilian population?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I said no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I've let this questioning and answering go on for a while. I think we're really now getting deep into the area of expert testimony, which we had some discussions about avoiding with respect to this witness who is being offered strictly as a fact witness and I've let it go because obviously given some of his experience at the time, some of it, I could tolerate, but this is really getting into the area of expertise where he's been asked to opine on documents and portions that I think we can hear more profitably from with respect to others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Fauveau? If you're moving to something different, you don't need to answer this. Let's --

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I finished with this sentence but I haven't finished with the directive, and I believe that we are dealing with the core of the Prosecution case against my client. We have before us a professional soldier of the VRS who has received at least one such document and who is able to tell us what at least one of those documents means and how we should interpret it. He can also tell us how he, as a member of the VRS, interpreted the said document. I don't think it has nothing to do with expert testimony. This is a commander of one of the brigades that was in the field at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have come to a conclusion, anyway, but it's time for the break, so we'll have a 20-minute break starting from now. I'll tell you exactly what the time is according, it is 16 hours 04 minutes. Please try to be punctual so that we start at 20 minutes from now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If I can clarify one thing which is very minor, Mr. Krgovic, can I draw your attention to page 19, lines starting from 23? It's a -- did you ask about General Miletic or General Gvero.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Miletic, and there is a reason for this, and this is one intercepted conversation where my client speaks of Miletic's daughter. That's why I put the question, because it is the position of the Prosecution that there was an ethnic prejudice involved there, and I wanted to raise the fact that Mr. Miletic's wife is a Croat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 20 minutes starting from now, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's decide this matter, this issue that was raised in the wake of Mr. Thayer's objection. Our position is as follows: If the intention of Madam Fauveau is to -- and for that matter, of any other counsel, is to ask this witness and any other witness opinion on documents that he was aware of at the time, also to elicit evidence of his understanding and interpretation of them, that is indeed an appropriate area of examination. However, if the intention is to draw from this witness general opinion evidence on the interpretation of military documents, orders, that would not be acceptable given that the witness is not here as an expert witness and he has not been qualified as such. In our judgement, in our considered opinion, the last question of Madam Fauveau falls within the first category and we are therefore allowing it. Go ahead, please, Madam Fauveau. I don't recall the witness -- the witness had answered. Yes, he had answered your question, so you can move to your next, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Could we show the witness page 1 of P107? That is still in e-court. No. It's P107. It was in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, you see at the top of this document, on the right-hand side, the words, "Krivaja 95."

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it correct that this name, Krivaja 95, is in fact the name that the Drina Corps command gave to the operation around Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This operation was carried out under that name.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Could we now show the witness the exhibit next to the witness, the directive, page 9, the page marked as 9 in B/C/S and 12 in English. Can we show the lower part of the page? Do you see among the tasks that were given to the Herzegovina Corps in the penultimate paragraph, something called Krivaja 95?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that in the section spelling out the assignments and guiding the activities of the Herzegovina Corps and the action for breaking through to the Neretva River valley is named Krivaja 95.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And that operation is in no way linked to Krivaja 95 as conducted around Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true. It is in no way linked to that action.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Can we now see the last page of this directive? Last page. No. This is the one-but-last, in fact. Where the signature is. Sir, if we look at point 8, para 8, of this directive, is it the case that all the decisions of the corps commanders were to be sent to the commander of the Main Staff of the VRS seven days prior to the execution of that operation?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's what item 8 stipulates.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And that concerns all the operations conducted based on this directive?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That applies to all the operations that the directive refers to as possible, and decisions related to these operations have to be sent seven days ahead of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And you've already told me that neither the preparatory order or the order for combat activities for 12th July were sent to the Main Staff of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The preparatory order and the ensuing order did not have to be sent to the commander of the Main Staff, if I recall very well. However, the decisions of commanders on the execution of certain operations have to be sent to the superior commander for approval. In this case, that's the -- in the case of the corps commander, they have to be sent to the commander of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: But in any case, the two orders that you received relating to the Krivaja 95 in Srebrenica were not sent to the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no obligation to send them.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: This directive that you have before you, it was signed by Radovan Karadzic, the Supreme Commander of the armed forces of Republika Srpska, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And you can see that it was drafted by Colonel Radivoje Miletic?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's what it says here.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it correct that the text of the directive was to be designed by Radovan Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The text of the directive is drafted by someone else, by those who formulate them on the basis of the conclusions of the assessment of the state of affairs in Republika Srpska at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I will rephrase my question. Is it correct that Colonel Miletic could write in that text of the directive only those things that were decided by Radovan Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What the Supreme Commander signs, regardless of the contents thereof, if it -- it is not the person who drafts the document who is held responsible for it but the one who signs it.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: So Radivoje Miletic could not have very well written his own ideas in this text?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course not. It is not up to the person drafting the document to present their own opinions in it or positions.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Can we now show the witness 5D361?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can I interrupt a minute, Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Trivic, you said -- answered to the counsel that the order Krivaja 95 didn't need to be sent to the Main Staff. You remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. There was no need for the written order to be sent. However, the decision therein had to be approved by the superior person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. You pre-empted my question. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If I understand you well, the order itself derived from a previous order or a confirmation from the Main Staff. Is that what you mean to tell us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Precisely. It derives from the decision approved by the commander. The order is formulated once a decision was made on the basis of a map. Now, the superior officer who drafts the order places the decision inside of it and then sends it to the subordinate persons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's very clear. Thank you. Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Now, concerning this operation, Krivaja 95, did you have occasion to see the map that was supposedly approved by the commander of the Main Staff of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw the map, together with the decision issued by the operations commander, namely the commander of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I believe we are on the same page here, that it was the map of the Drina Corps commander. But you never saw a decision or a map approved by Ratko Mladic concerning the Krivaja 95 operation conducted around Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if I saw it or not, but I believe I did. It contained the axes of engagement and assignments of units. As a rule, the commanders' reconnaissance that I mentioned a day ago was the occasion when I saw the map, at the briefing there.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you remember who signed that map that you think you saw?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. As a rule it was to be signed by the person who drafted it, corps commander, and it is approved in the upper right-hand corner, the commanding officer, superior commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: But you don't recall seeing the signature of Ratko Mladic on the map you saw?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, what you have before you, is that the directive 7/1, issued by the Main Staff of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Can we show the witness page 5 of this directive, and in English it's also page 5. Sir, do you see item 5.3? It relates to the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Can you read it to yourself, these two paragraphs that concern the tasks of the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it correct that this directive does not contain any plan of action against the enclaves?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. That's correct. What is mentioned here is the defence and active combat activities around the enclaves, to prevent the enemy from breaking through along certain axes and to engage them with as many forces as possible, to keep them engaged. There is no mention of the assignment that was to be carried out within Krivaja 95 operation.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it correct that the commander of the Main Staff of the VRS, in this directive, changed or adjusted the tasks entrusted to the Drina Corps by the Supreme Commander, Radovan Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me go back again to the role of directives as combat documents. I've already said that directives are not binding documents. They are not assignments. They are merely guidelines, food for thought, about certain parts of the battlefields, and they normally suggest that such and such problems be solved. In directive 7/1, it was the assessment of the commander of the Main Staff that, at that point in time, both for the Main Staff and the VRS, there were tasks of greater priority, of higher priority than this, and he relinquished the idea, the idea that had been entertained by the directive and concluded that some other matters had to be dealt with as a priority. There was, however, a possibility for the corps commands to decide whether they wanted to engage forces within their own areas of responsibility. Three months later, it is said -- this shows that the corps commander fully comprehended the customary role of a directive as merely a set of guidelines as to how to proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I'm going to move on to the events that just preceded the operation and just before you entered Srebrenica. Last Friday and yesterday you said that just after you entered Srebrenica on the 5th of July, there was a meeting at which Colonel Vicic was present.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it correct that Colonel Vicic himself was not able himself to issue orders to brigade commanders?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The role of Colonel Vicic as an operations officer was to acquaint the commanders and convey to them the order and assignment set by the commander. He was not able to issue his own assignments.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You remember a meeting that you had on the 5th of July, 1995, just before the operation around Srebrenica began?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And when you attended that meeting, you didn't see a map on which unit positions and movements were drawn in?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall seeing it.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You said yesterday that you had passed by Slapovici. Is it correct that at Slapovici you didn't find any Muslim units?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. I did not come across any defence units of the 28th Division.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And you didn't see anything burning, any houses burning, in Slapovici?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. All the houses were intact.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: When you were passing by, did you see any burning haystacks? Was that used to mark your positions?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was a standard procedure, given the lie of the land. That was almost the only way to see the lines reached by the units.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it correct that when you entered Slapovici, the village was empty, there were no residents there?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That village was completely empty. There was no one there.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Could we then say that the population of Slapovici had pulled out before the units of the VRS entered the village?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And when you arrived at Srebrenica, you didn't find the civilian population of Srebrenica either?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My unit did not go into Srebrenica. This was not our assignment. There may have been individual cases out of curiosity. There was no population. There were several elderly persons moving about on foot. Evidently, during the day, measures had been taken for the population to pull out into the area under the command of the UN forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: When you say that measures had been taken for the population to pull out, you're talking about the measures taken by the Muslim authorities?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly it was them who took the measures, together with the town command and UNPROFOR forces for the population to pull out.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You personally did enter Srebrenica. Did you hear that the few persons who stayed in Srebrenica were to assemble at the local stadium?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All these persons were directed to go toward Potocari, as far as I heard. It turned out to be that way when I took along two grandmothers who were waving at me to stop as I was driving in my vehicle. I put them into my vehicle and drove them over to the place where the population was gathering. They, of course, thanked me for it and got out of the vehicle and stayed there in that area.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And these two grannies asked you to take them to Potocari themselves; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: When you met with General Mladic at Srebrenica, is it correct that General Mladic gave units the order to continue on to Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And that order was not carried out, was it?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of those present, I can't say who, I remember it being mentioned and besides, we saw it in the video footage yesterday, that he issued the task of moving in the direction of Bratunac. I told him that I had already been executing assignments pursuant to the orders I received before and somebody suggested that the units should not head for Potocari since the civilian population was gathering there, and that was the end of the story. General Mladic accepted the suggestion.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And in fact, General Mladic accepted that suggestion so as to avoid any mixing of the Muslim civilian population with the troops of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. One could make that conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I would like to show you 6D127. It's a combat report from your unit. You have already seen it. Is it right that para 1 -- I suppose that you were a brigade commander and as such you had occasion to see a lot of combat orders of this format.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it correct that para 1 of this report describes the situation in the area of your brigade on the 15th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was the situation of the day, put in so many words, in the area of responsibility of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And this report was written based on the report that the brigade received from battalions?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: The person who wrote up combat reports in your brigade was the operations officer, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the duty officer in the operations organ.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: If you look at items 3, 4 and 6 of this report, we see references to the security situation, to the morale of troops, and the situation with logistical support?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it correct that the officer who wrote up this report had to consult with officers from these respective sectors in order to include their inputs in their respective areas in his report?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the level of the brigade command, yes, and that also went for the superior commands.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Can we see the top of the page? This report was sent to the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it correct that the brigade did not send any reports to the Main Staff of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true. The -- there is the obligation to send reports to the command that is immediately superior to the one issuing the reports.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it correct that you, as brigade commander, had no direct contact whatsoever with officers of the Main Staff of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I did not in any capacity that I held.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And during the operation in Srebrenica and Zepa, you never had occasion to contact with General Miletic, did you?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not contact with him during operation Krivaja 95 and operation Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And if General Miletic had given you an order, you wouldn't have carried it out, would you?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Miletic, or rather the operations organ of the Main Staff, was not in a position to issue orders, and I believe that he acted accordingly, and I would not have carried out such an order had it been issued by him or by somebody else. There are rules governing relations between superiors and subordinates, senior and junior officers, in this case, the superior command, and no structure will circumvent one step in the chain of command and, for instance, issue orders to the second subordinate structure.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you know who was the head of the Main Staff of the VRS in July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The chief of the Main Staff, throughout the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina, of the VRS was General Milovanic.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And you know that in July, 1995, General Milovanovic was in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that he was not present in the area where the Main Staff was stationed. He was in the area of Bosnian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it correct that as long as General Milovanovic was on the territory of Republika Srpska, even if he was not in the headquarters of the Main Staff, he remained Chief of Staff of the Main Staff of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And in July, 1995, there was no need whatsoever for anyone to stand in for General Milovanovic in his position of Chief of Staff of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, again, at this point I think we would need some foundation laid as to whether this witness has the familiarity at the time with what was going on in the Main Staff to know whether this is in fact the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Witness, before I ask you, are you in a position to answer this question in any case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe I am. If you'll allow me to explain why I believe I am, the theatres of war where the VRS army was engaged covered the entire territory of Republika Srpska. General Milovanovic, the commander of the Main Staff or someone else, chief of the security offices would act throughout the war in his respective capacity, namely that of the Chief of Staff, regardless of his whereabouts in the theatre of war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, do you know that General Milovanovic was the immediate superior of General Miletic?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The operations organ or rather the operations administration was attached to the headquarters commanded by General Milovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And since in July, 1995 General Milovanovic discharged his functions, could we say that General Miletic could not take any decisions without consulting with or without receiving the approval of his immediate superior, General Milovanovic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, can you answer that question? Are you in a position to answer that question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe I am. If you'll allow me, I studied the art of warfare in my post-graduate studies. I also took part in a research team as part of the General Staff of the JNA in Croatia. I dealt with these matters. I also dealt with these matters as I was studying the theory for my post-graduate studies. I can answer this question in principle because general --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, again, we have no objection to expert testimony being presented on this and other related issues, but what we clearly have here again is this witness continuing to be used as an expert witness by the Defence and using cross-examination, leading questions, to elicit expert testimony.
